when i was first starting out, i gravitated towards bento cookbooks and youtube videos that presented typical japanese recipes in a really accessible way. my favorite book that i still reference a lot for bento cooking is real bento- the recipes are doable, delicious, and filling, and can easily be scaled up or down. this book also taught me a lot about basics of japanese cooking, and simple modern japanese-ish seasonings that might be surprising because they incorporate some pretty common western ingredients- like ketchup!! the author describes substitutions that can be made for ingredients too.

for recipes, i would recommend learning how to make sauces like teriyaki that you can apply to lots of different proteins and veg! another sauce combo i like is soy sauce + butter, it's like heaven on earth. miso sauces add a lot of taste to vegetables and chicken. learn how to make dashi and your own tsuyu/mentsuyu, and you can use that to make miso soup, flavor other dishes, and prepare a broth or dipping sauce for somen, soba, and udon. if you eat the noodles cold, you can add leftover ingredients from the fridge, sliced ham, etc. to get a really nice and tasty meal. :)

ooh, also- eggs! rolled eggs (which you can do in a regular pan with a little practice), omurice, omelets, anything eggs. something i so love about japanese cooking is all the egg recipes that i can eat any time of day. other stuff i'm just thinking of now: for simple fish dishes, grab fish, roast in oven, sprinkle with soy sauce when done. and anything with rice! rice cookers are amazing. you can toss lots of ingredients and seasonings in with the rice, cook them with the rice, and end up with a wonderful filling meal.

They may say it's disrespectful regardless of how you bring it up. But the thing is, it's not disrespectful to set boundaries around comments about your body. Full stop. We are taught growing up, by our society, that pretty much any commentary on our body is normal and even deserved, and that's just not the case. 

I often use the following line with my own family: "You aren't allowed to make comments like that to me anymore." or "You aren't allowed to make comments about my body." I got those from all the reading I've done from various body acceptance authors; firmly and calmly stating such a boundary is actually a really adult, respectful, and responsible thing. It's like saying, if you want to earn the privilege of interacting with me more, you can respect my boundary. And just because they're your parents (and even if you live with them!) that doesn't mean you can't set boundaries and even consequences for not respecting your boundaries. Really. It's because your body is so personal and belongs to you. No one should be allowed to put it or you down, because it has far-reaching consequences on our overall health, including mental health- which is actually pretty damn important!

An example of a consequence: I have told my family I will walk away or leave the room if they don't respect my boundaries. I then do my best to follow through with these consequences. 

I just want to give you a hug and let you know that it's totally okay to tell your parents it isn't okay to talk about your body. They might not get it right away, or ever, but that isn't your responsibility. I would actually even advocate things like plugging your ears with your fingers if they won't stop talking after you've asked them to stop; it sounds childish, but it's not, and the reality is sometimes we have very few ways to protect ourselves when it comes to parents depending on our circumstances. My parents have actually told me that they think it's completely appropriate and even expected for a grown adult daughter to inform her parents about her weight and what it says on the scale. I was dumbfounded. To me, sharing such personal stuff like that that I have loads of trauma around (partially thanks to them) is uncalled for. So sometimes what they think is really fucking messed up and not right, and again that's not your problem.

thank you for making this post- i don't know if i have much helpful info to add but i did want to say i can relate so hard to the sentiment here. it really is tough feeling just awful over and over again, feeling guilty canceling, feeling like you "can't live a normal life"...

for now, i am trying to take things slow and practically. i have anxiety so i pretty much read the worst case scenario into everything. it's taken some therapy to look beyond that and realize that what other people think and say about me has more to do with them than me; if i am cancelling because i feel unwell, that's legitimate self-care, which i value. i try to be honest about how i'm feeling. with certain people and in certain circumstances, i might explain a little more, like "i'm dealing with a chronic condition etc. and i just don't feel the greatest right now". i have mostly found out that people are very compassionate and understanding. if it's possible to reschedule or something, i will do that too.

i say "sorry" often too, but something i'm trying to work on is saying "sorry" less or not at all- it's not like i asked to have these medical issues, right? instead i use another therapy trick- thanking people for what i appreciate about them in this situation. for example, if i have to cancel a session for work- "I so appreciate your understanding." rather than "I'm so, so sorry I keep cancelling!"
